decks.title: Equilibrium Output, Multiplier and Problems of Demand — Part 1: Equilibrium and the Multiplier
goals: Find equilibrium income by the AD = AS and S = I approaches, from a schedule and a diagram
Explain how output adjusts when planned spending and output differ
Calculate the investment multiplier and the change in income, and explain its working round by round

slides.heading: Equilibrium Output and the Multiplier
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how **equilibrium income** is fixed, how the economy **adjusts**, and how a change in investment is **multiplied** into a bigger change in income.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: aggregate demand and supply, the two approaches to equilibrium, adjustment, the multiplier and its rounds of spending
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: An economy produces goods, and households and firms plan to buy them. When planned buying matches production, output settles. In this part we find that settling point, called equilibrium income, in two ways. Then we see how a single new investment can raise income by several times its own size, through rounds of spending.

slides.heading: Equilibrium: planned spending equals output
slides.body_md: In a two-sector economy **AD = C + I** and **AS = Y** (the value of output). **Equilibrium income** is the income at which **AD = AS**.

rows: Planned spending buys exactly what is produced
The leakage from spending is matched by the injection

visual.alt: Table of the two approaches to equilibrium income: aggregate demand equal to aggregate supply, where planned spending buys all output; and saving equal to investment, where the leakage from spending is matched by the injection
visual.caption: AD = C + I and AS = C + S, so both conditions pick the same income.

slides.narration: Aggregate demand is the total that households plan to consume plus what firms plan to invest. Aggregate supply is the value of what is produced, which equals the income earned. Income is in equilibrium when these two are equal. Because income is either spent or saved, the same point is where planned saving equals planned investment.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a schedule for Tarangpur
slides.body_md: Imagined economy, ₹ crore: **C = 60 + 0.8Y**, **I = 40**. Find the income where AD = Y.
bullets: Step 1 — AD = C + I at each income.
Step 2 — Compare AD with Y.
Step 3 — AD = Y at **500**; check S = I there.

visual.alt: Schedule of the imagined economy of Tarangpur for incomes 0 to 700: consumption 60, 140, 220, 300, 380, 460, 540, 620; saving -60, -40, -20, 0, 20, 40, 60, 80; investment 40 throughout; aggregate demand 100, 180, 260, 340, 420, 500, 580, 660. Aggregate demand equals income only at 500, where saving also equals investment
visual.caption: Imagined figures, ₹ crore.

slides.narration: Work down the schedule. At an income of four hundred, consumption is three hundred and eighty, so aggregate demand is four hundred and twenty, more than output. At six hundred, demand is only five hundred and eighty, less than output. Only at five hundred does demand equal income, and saving there is forty, matching investment.

slides.heading: The AD = AS diagram
slides.body_md: AS is the **forty-five degree line** (spending = income). AD starts at autonomous spending and is **flatter** (slope = MPC). Equilibrium is at **E**.

Where it cuts the forty-five degree line, at five hundred, the economy is in equilibrium.

slides.narration: The second approach looks at leakages and injections. Saving is money not spent, a leakage. Investment is spending added by firms, an injection. Saving starts negative at low incomes, crosses zero at the break-even income of three hundred, and meets investment of forty at an income of five hundred, the same equilibrium as before.

slides.heading: Below equilibrium: output rises
slides.body_md: If **AD > AS** (**I > S**), buyers take more than is produced. **Stocks fall** below plan, so firms **produce more**.

visual.alt: Flow of adjustment when aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply: stocks run down, firms raise output, and income rises to equilibrium
visual.caption: Below equilibrium

slides.narration: Suppose output is below equilibrium. Planned spending is greater than what is being produced, so shops and warehouses find their stocks shrinking unexpectedly. Firms respond by producing more and hiring more workers. Income rises, and it keeps rising until planned spending equals output again.

slides.heading: Above equilibrium: output falls
slides.body_md: If **AD < AS** (**S > I**), part of output is **unsold**. Stocks **pile up** beyond plan, so firms **cut production**.

visual.alt: Flow of adjustment when aggregate demand is less than aggregate supply: unsold stocks pile up, firms cut output, and income falls to equilibrium
visual.caption: Above equilibrium

slides.narration: Now suppose output is above equilibrium. Planned spending falls short of production, so unsold goods pile up beyond what firms planned to hold. Firms cut production and jobs. As income falls, saving falls too, until saving once more equals investment at equilibrium.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the diagram
slides.body_md: To the left of equilibrium, AD lies **above** the forty-five degree line. This means…
slides.narration: Remember that any point on the forty-five degree line has spending equal to output.

slides.heading: The investment multiplier
slides.body_md: **k = ΔY ÷ ΔI**. A rise in investment raises income by **k times** as much. **k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPS**.

visual.alt: Table of the multiplier for marginal propensities to consume of 0, 0.5, 0.75, 0.8 and 0.9: the multipliers are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10; the multiplier rises as the marginal propensity to consume rises
visual.caption: The higher the MPC, the larger the multiplier; k is never below 1.

slides.narration: The investment multiplier tells us how many times income rises for a given rise in investment. It depends on how much of any extra income people spend. If they spend nothing extra, the multiplier is one. If they spend most of it, the multiplier is large. That is why it equals one divided by the marginal propensity to save.

slides.heading: Quick check: from the multiplier to the MPS
slides.body_md: An imagined hill economy has a multiplier of 4. Its MPS must be…
slides.narration: The multiplier is one divided by the marginal propensity to save. Turn that round.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: rounds of extra income
slides.body_md: A metro project adds **₹100 crore** of investment; **MPC = 0.8**.
bullets: Round 1: 100 paid as wages and to suppliers.
Round 2: 0.8 × 100 = 80 spent, becoming others' income.
Round 3: 64; and so on.

visual.alt: Table of multiplier rounds after investment of 100 crore rupees with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8: rounds of 100, 80, 64, 51.2 and so on, adding up to 500
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Follow the money. The project pays one hundred crore to workers and suppliers. They spend eighty per cent of it, eighty crore, which becomes income for shopkeepers and farmers. They in turn spend eighty per cent of that, sixty-four crore, and so on. The rounds get smaller, and together they add up to five hundred crore.

visual.caption: ΔI = 20 shifts AD up by 20; ΔY = k × ΔI = 5 × 20 = 100.

slides.narration: In Tarangpur, a port company invests an extra twenty crore. The aggregate demand line shifts up by twenty, from AD one to AD two. The new equilibrium is at six hundred, one hundred higher. Twenty crore of new investment has raised income by one hundred crore, five times as much, because the multiplier is five.

slides.heading: The multiplier works both ways
slides.body_md: A **fall** in investment lowers income by **k times** the fall. The range of k is **1 to infinity**: 1 when MPC = 0, very large as MPC nears 1.

nodes.label: Incomes of workers and suppliers rise

visual.alt: Flow of the multiplier process: investment raises the incomes of workers and suppliers, a share equal to the marginal propensity to consume is spent and becomes others' income, the rounds shrink, and the total rise in income is the multiplier times the rise in investment
visual.caption: How the multiplier works

slides.narration: The same chain works in reverse. If investment falls, workers and suppliers lose income, spend less, and others lose income too. So income falls by the multiplier times the fall in investment. The multiplier is never below one, and it grows larger the closer the marginal propensity to consume comes to one.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Unplanned stock changes push output back
From 1 upwards; larger when MPC is higher

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: equilibrium where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply or saving equals investment; unplanned changes in stocks push output back; the multiplier is one over the marginal propensity to save; income changes by the multiplier times the change in investment

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Equilibrium income is where aggregate demand equals aggregate supply, or equivalently where saving equals investment. Unplanned changes in stocks push output towards that point. A change in investment changes income by the multiplier times as much, and the multiplier is one over the marginal propensity to save.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **both** conditions: AD = AS and S = I; show they give the same income.
On diagrams, label the **forty-five degree line**, the **AD** line and the point **E** with its income.
Do not confuse **break-even income** (C = Y) with **equilibrium** (C + I = Y).
For the multiplier, write **k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC)** and then **ΔY = k × ΔI**, with units.
Explain adjustment through **unplanned changes in stocks**.

rows: Planned spending buys exactly what is produced
The leakage from spending is matched by the injection

visual.alt: Table of the two approaches to equilibrium income: aggregate demand equal to aggregate supply, where planned spending buys all output; and saving equal to investment, where the leakage from spending is matched by the injection
visual.caption: AD = C + I and AS = C + S, so both conditions pick the same income.

slides.narration: Examiners reward complete answers. Give both conditions for equilibrium and show they agree. Label every line on your diagram and the equilibrium income. Do not mix up the break-even point of the consumption function with equilibrium. Write the multiplier formula before using it. And always explain adjustment through stocks that are larger or smaller than planned.

decks.title: Equilibrium Output, Multiplier and Problems of Demand — Part 2: Full Employment and Problems of Demand
goals: Explain full employment and involuntary unemployment
Show inflationary and deflationary gaps on a diagram and calculate them
Explain the causes and effects of excess and deficient demand, and suggest fiscal and monetary measures

slides.heading: Full Employment and Problems of Demand
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **full employment**, why equilibrium can fall **short** of it, **excess** and **deficient** demand, and the **measures** that correct them.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: full employment, underemployment equilibrium, deflationary gap, inflationary gap, and fiscal and monetary cures
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Equilibrium income is not always the income a country wants. It may leave willing workers without jobs, or it may push prices up. In this part we compare equilibrium with full employment, measure the gap between them, and see how governments and central banks can close it.

slides.heading: Full employment
slides.body_md: **Full employment**: all who are **able and willing to work at the prevailing wage** have work. It allows some **frictional** and **voluntary** idleness.

rows: All able and willing to work at the going wage have jobs
A town where any willing worker finds work at the going wage
Willing to work at the going wage but cannot find work
A trained welder who would accept the going wage, with no openings
A nurse moving to a new hospital next month
Not willing to work at the going wage
Someone who chooses to wait for a far higher wage

visual.alt: Table of employment terms: full employment, where all who are able and willing to work at the going wage have jobs; involuntary unemployment, where people willing to work at the going wage cannot find work; frictional unemployment between jobs; and voluntary unemployment of those unwilling to work at the going wage

slides.narration: Full employment does not mean that every single person is working. It means that everyone who is able and willing to work at the going wage has a job. People moving between jobs, or choosing not to work at that wage, may still be idle. Involuntary unemployment, people who would work at the going wage but find no job, is what full employment rules out.

slides.heading: Equilibrium below full employment
slides.body_md: Keynes: equilibrium is fixed by **AD**. If planned spending is low, AD = AS **below** full-employment output: an **underemployment equilibrium**.

nodes.label: AD meets AS below full-employment output
No pressure on firms to expand

visual.alt: Flow of an underemployment equilibrium: low planned spending makes aggregate demand meet aggregate supply below full-employment output, firms have no reason to expand, and involuntary unemployment persists
visual.caption: Keynes: equilibrium need not be at full employment

slides.narration: Keynes argued that nothing guarantees equilibrium at full employment. Equilibrium is wherever planned spending equals output. If households and firms plan to spend too little, output settles at a level that employs fewer people than want work. Firms have no reason to expand, so involuntary unemployment can last.

slides.heading: Quick check: excess demand at full employment
slides.body_md: An imagined economy at full employment sees demand jump. What happens mainly?
slides.narration: If there are no idle workers or machines, can output rise? What else can give?

slides.body_md: **Deflationary gap** = full-employment output − AD at that output. Hiranagar: **400 − 360 = 40**.

visual.caption: Same AD, Yf = 250: AD exceeds output at full employment by 20.

slides.narration: Suppose instead that full employment were reached at only two hundred and fifty. Planned spending at that output is two hundred and seventy, twenty more than can be produced. That excess, measured at full employment, is the inflationary gap. Since output cannot rise further, the extra demand pushes up prices.

slides.heading: Causes and effects of the two gaps
columns:
**Excess demand** (inflationary gap)

- Causes: more public spending, easy credit, higher exports, lower saving.
- Effects: prices rise; no extra output or jobs.

**Deficient demand** (deflationary gap)

- Causes: lower investment or exports, more saving, tight credit.
- Effects: output and jobs fall; involuntary unemployment.

rows: More public spending, easy credit, higher exports, lower saving
Lower investment, lower exports, higher saving, tighter credit

visual.alt: Table comparing excess and deficient demand: causes such as more public spending or easy credit against lower investment or exports; effects on output, prices and jobs

slides.narration: Excess demand comes from spending growing faster than capacity, for example through easy credit or large public spending. Its main effect is rising prices. Deficient demand comes from spending falling, for example when investment or exports drop. Its main effect is lost output and jobs.

slides.heading: Fiscal measures
slides.body_md: **Fiscal policy** uses **government spending** and **taxes**. Against **excess** demand: spend less, tax more. Against **deficient** demand: spend more, tax less.

visual.alt: Table of corrective measures: against excess demand, cut government spending, raise taxes, raise the repo rate, the reserve ratios and margins, and sell securities; against deficient demand, do the opposite
visual.caption: Directions only; no current policy values are stated.

slides.narration: The government can change aggregate demand through its own budget. To cool excess demand, it can cut its spending and raise taxes, so people have less to spend. To lift deficient demand, it can spend more on public works and cut taxes. Public spending also works through the multiplier.

slides.heading: Monetary measures
slides.body_md: The **central bank** changes the **cost and availability of credit**: repo rate and bank rate, **CRR** and **SLR**, **open market operations**, and selective tools such as **margin requirements**.

visual.alt: Flow of a repo rate cut: banks get funds more cheaply, lower their loan rates, households and firms borrow and spend more, and aggregate demand rises
visual.caption: Monetary transmission (deficient demand)

slides.narration: The central bank works through credit. Raising the repo rate or the reserve ratios, or selling securities, makes bank credit dearer and scarcer, which cools excess demand. Cutting them, or buying securities, makes credit cheaper and more plentiful, which helps when demand is deficient. Selective tools like margins target lending for particular goods.

slides.heading: Quick check: the CRR
slides.body_md: To control excess demand, the central bank raises the CRR. How does this help?
slides.narration: If banks must keep more of their deposits as cash with the central bank, what happens to their lending?

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how much spending closes the gap?
slides.body_md: Hiranagar: deflationary gap **40**, **k = 2.5**. Extra spending of **40** raises income by 2.5 × 40 = **100**, from 300 to **400**.
bullets: The extra spending needed equals the **gap**, not the shortfall in income.
Spending the whole shortfall (100) would overshoot full employment and cause excess demand.

visual.alt: Flow showing that extra spending of 40 crore rupees in Hiranagar, multiplied by 2.5, raises income by 100 to the full-employment level of 400
visual.caption: Closing the gap

slides.narration: A common error is to think the government must add the whole shortfall in income, one hundred crore. But the multiplier is two and a half. Adding just forty crore of spending raises income by one hundred, exactly to full employment. Adding a hundred would overshoot and create excess demand.

slides.heading: Quick check: a fiscal error
slides.body_md: True or false? Cutting income-tax rates suits an economy with excess demand.
slides.narration: Ask whether a tax cut raises or lowers spending.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 2

rows: AD can settle below full employment
AD > output at full employment: prices rise
AD < output at full employment: jobs lost
Fiscal and monetary tools, in opposite directions for each gap

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: full employment, underemployment equilibrium, inflationary and deflationary gaps, and fiscal and monetary cures

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Full employment means no involuntary unemployment, but equilibrium can settle below it. An inflationary gap is excess demand at full employment and raises prices; a deflationary gap is deficient demand and costs jobs. Fiscal and monetary tools correct each gap when used in the right direction.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Measure gaps **at full-employment output**, not at equilibrium.
On the gap diagram, mark **Yf**, the forty-five degree line and AD, and shade the **vertical** gap.
For measures, always give the **direction** (raise or cut) and **how** it changes AD.
Excess demand raises **prices**, not output; deficient demand cuts **output and jobs**.
Do not quote current policy rates; explain the mechanism.

visual.caption: Directions only; no current policy values are stated.

slides.narration: Measure every gap at the full-employment output. Draw the gap as a vertical distance at that output. When you suggest a measure, state whether it is raised or cut and how that changes aggregate demand. Remember which gap affects prices and which affects jobs. And explain how a tool works rather than quoting a current rate.

sections.heading: 2. Equilibrium income: S = I, and adjustment
sections.body_md:
- AS = C + S and AD = C + I, so **AD = AS** is the same as **planned S = planned I**.
- **AD > AS (I > S)**: stocks fall below plan, firms expand, income rises.
- **AD < AS (S > I)**: unsold stocks build up, firms cut back, income falls.
- The adjustment stops only at equilibrium.

key_terms.definition_md: Income not passed on as spending, such as saving.
Spending added from outside consumption, such as investment.
A rise or fall in stocks that firms did not intend; the signal that output is not at equilibrium.

sections.heading: 3. The investment multiplier
sections.body_md:
- **k = ΔY ÷ ΔI = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) = 1 ÷ MPS**.
- **Working**: new investment becomes income; a share (the MPC) is spent and becomes others' income; rounds shrink by the MPC; their sum is k × ΔI.
- Imagined metro project: ΔI = 100, MPC = 0.8: rounds 100, 80, 64, 51.2…, total **500**.
- **Range**: k = 1 when MPC = 0; k grows without limit as MPC approaches 1. It works **backwards** too.
- Tarangpur: ΔI = 20 raises income from 500 to **600**.

key_terms.definition_md: The number of times income changes for a given change in investment.
The share of extra income that is saved; the multiplier is its reciprocal.

sections.heading: 4. Full employment and involuntary unemployment
sections.body_md:
- **Full employment**: no involuntary unemployment; frictional and voluntary idleness can remain.
- **Involuntary unemployment**: willing to work at the prevailing wage, but no work available.
- In Keynesian theory equilibrium depends on **effective demand**, so the economy can rest at an **underemployment equilibrium** with output below its full-employment level.

key_terms.definition_md: A state in which all who are able and willing to work at the going wage are employed.
Unemployment of people willing to work at the going wage who cannot find jobs.
An equilibrium in which output is below the full-employment level.

sections.heading: 5. Excess and deficient demand
sections.body_md:
- **Inflationary gap** (excess demand) = AD at full-employment output − that output. Main effect: **prices rise**, since output cannot.
- **Deflationary gap** (deficient demand) = full-employment output − AD there. Effects: **output and employment fall**, involuntary unemployment.
- Imagined Hiranagar, AD = 120 + 0.6Y: with Yf = 400, gap = **40** (deflationary); with Yf = 250, gap = **20** (inflationary).
- To close a deflationary gap, extra spending equal to the **gap** is enough: k × gap = 2.5 × 40 = 100.

key_terms.definition_md: The excess of aggregate demand over output at full employment.
The shortfall of aggregate demand below output at full employment.

sections.heading: 6. Measures to correct excess and deficient demand
sections.body_md:
- **Fiscal**: government spending and taxes (and public borrowing). Excess demand: spend less, tax more. Deficient demand: spend more, tax less.
- **Monetary (quantitative)**: repo and bank rate, CRR and SLR, open market operations. Excess demand: raise rates and ratios, sell securities. Deficient demand: the reverse.
- **Monetary (qualitative)**: margin requirements, credit rationing, moral suasion, direct action — aimed at particular uses of credit.
- Fiscal steps change AD **directly**; monetary steps work **through borrowing**, which may respond slowly when expectations are weak.

- Calling the break-even income (C = Y) the equilibrium income.
- Measuring a gap at the equilibrium income instead of at full-employment output.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined two-sector economy of Tarangpur, which condition must hold at the equilibrium level of income?

options.text_md: Consumption equals income
Planned aggregate demand equals aggregate supply (planned spending equals output)
Investment equals consumption
Saving is zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Planned aggregate demand equals aggregate supply (planned spending equals output). Output settles where what households and firms plan to spend equals what is produced, AD = AS. C = Y is the break-even point of the consumption function; it is not the equilibrium unless investment is zero.

questions.stem_md: A student of an imagined Shillong college studies equilibrium income by the leakage–injection method. In a two-sector economy the condition she uses is

options.text_md: saving equals consumption
investment equals income
saving equals income
planned saving equals planned investment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** planned saving equals planned investment. In a two-sector economy AD = C + I and AS = C + S, so AD = AS is the same as planned S = planned I.

questions.stem_md: Shops in the imagined town of Tarangpur find unsold goods piling up beyond the stocks they had planned. This tells us that at the current output

options.text_md: aggregate demand is less than aggregate supply, so output will fall
aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply, so output will rise
the economy is at equilibrium
planned investment exceeds planned saving

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** aggregate demand is less than aggregate supply, so output will fall. Unplanned piling up of stocks means buyers are taking less than is produced: AD < AS (planned S > planned I). Firms respond by cutting production, so income falls towards equilibrium.

questions.stem_md: Traders in an imagined Bhopal wholesale market find their stocks running down faster than planned at the present level of output. What happens next in the economy?

options.text_md: Firms cut production, so income falls
Prices and output stay unchanged
Firms raise production, so income and employment rise
Planned saving rises above planned investment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Firms raise production, so income and employment rise. Stocks running down unexpectedly means AD > AS. Firms expand output to rebuild stocks, so income rises until AD = AS.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined economy of Tarangpur, C = 60 + 0.8Y and investment is ₹40 crore. What is its equilibrium income?

options.text_md: ₹300 crore
₹100 crore
₹500 crore
₹600 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹500 crore. Y = (a + I) ÷ (1 − b) = (60 + 40) ÷ 0.2 = 500. ₹300 crore is the break-even income where C = Y, and ₹100 crore is only autonomous spending.

questions.stem_md: On an income–expenditure diagram of an imagined island economy, at an income to the left of equilibrium the aggregate demand curve lies above the forty-five degree line. This means

options.text_md: planned spending exceeds output, so output tends to rise
output exceeds planned spending, so output tends to fall
saving exceeds investment
the economy is at full employment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** planned spending exceeds output, so output tends to rise. Every point on the forty-five degree line has spending equal to output. Where AD lies above it, planned spending is greater than output, so firms expand production.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** On an income–expenditure diagram, the aggregate supply curve is drawn as a forty-five degree line through the origin.

**Reason (R):** Aggregate supply is the value of output, which equals income, so every point on the line is equidistant from the two axes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since AS = Y, plotting AS against Y on equal scales traces the line where the vertical and horizontal distances are equal, the forty-five degree line.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When planned saving exceeds planned investment, national income tends to fall.

**Reason (R):** When planned saving exceeds planned investment, firms find their stocks running down below the planned level.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: saving above investment means AD < AS, so output and income fall. R is false: stocks pile up above the planned level (they would run down if investment exceeded saving).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the imagined economy of Tarangpur (C = 60 + 0.8Y, I = 40), equilibrium income is the income at which consumption equals income.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. C = Y at the break-even income of ₹300 crore, where saving is zero. Equilibrium needs C + I = Y, which happens at ₹500 crore, where saving equals investment of 40.

questions.stem_md: In a two-sector economy, equilibrium income is reached where planned saving equals planned ___.
questions.solution_md: S = I: saving is the leakage and investment the injection; equilibrium is where they are equal.

questions.stem_md: An imagined coastal economy of Kanakpur has C = 40 + 0.75Y and planned investment of ₹60 crore. Find its equilibrium income (in ₹ crore).
In the imagined economy of Tarangpur (C = 60 + 0.8Y), equilibrium income is ₹500 crore. What is planned saving at this income (in ₹ crore)?
questions.solution_md: S = −60 + 0.2 × 500 = 40, equal to investment of 40, as it must be at equilibrium.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which the imagined economy of Tarangpur moves to equilibrium when its output is below the equilibrium level.

options.text_md: Stocks of goods run down below the planned level
Income rises until planned spending equals output
Planned spending is greater than current output
Firms increase production and hire more workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (a) → (d) → (b). Excess demand comes first, it shows up as falling stocks, firms respond by producing more, and income rises until AD = AS.

questions.stem_md: State the two approaches to determining equilibrium income in a two-sector economy, giving the condition used in each, as a study note for an imagined Patna coaching class.
questions.solution_md: Name each approach with its condition.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **aggregate demand–aggregate supply approach**: equilibrium where **AD = AS**, that is, planned C + I equals output.
2. The **saving–investment approach**: equilibrium where **planned S = planned I**, leakages equal injections.

questions.stem_md: Show why the conditions AD = AS and S = I give the same equilibrium income in the imagined two-sector economy of Tarangpur.
questions.solution_md: AD = C + I and AS = C + S; cancel C.

answer.model_answer_md: Aggregate demand is **C + I** and aggregate supply, the income earned, is spent or saved: **C + S**. Setting **C + I = C + S** and cancelling C leaves **I = S**. So the two conditions describe the **same income**.

marking_scheme.step: AD = C + I and AS = C + S

questions.stem_md:
The table below shows consumption and investment in the imagined economy of Tarangpur. Calculate aggregate demand at each income and find equilibrium income.

| Income Y (₹ crore) | Consumption C | Investment I |
|---|---|---|
| 300 | 300 | 40 |
| 400 | 380 | 40 |
| 500 | 460 | 40 |
| 600 | 540 | 40 |
questions.solution_md: Add C and I; find AD = Y.

answer.model_answer_md: **AD = C + I:** 300 + 40 = **340**; 380 + 40 = **420**; 460 + 40 = **500**; 540 + 40 = **580**. Equilibrium is where **AD = Y**: at **₹500 crore**, AD is also 500. Below it AD exceeds output (420 at 400) and above it AD falls short (580 at 600).

questions.stem_md: In the imagined economy of Tarangpur, at an income of ₹600 crore planned saving is ₹60 crore while planned investment is ₹40 crore. Explain how income adjusts and where it settles.
questions.solution_md: S > I: AD < AS, stocks pile up, output falls to S = I.

answer.model_answer_md: Saving (60) is **greater** than investment (40), so the **leakage exceeds the injection**: planned spending (580) is **less than output** (600). Unsold goods **pile up**, so firms **cut output** and income falls. As income falls, saving falls too, until **S = I = 40** at **₹500 crore**.

questions.stem_md:
The imagined economy of Tarangpur has the consumption function C = 60 + 0.8Y and planned investment of ₹40 crore.

(a) Find equilibrium income by the AD = AS approach and check it by the S = I approach. [3]
(b) Describe the adjustment if the economy were producing ₹400 crore. [2]
questions.solution_md: Solve AD = Y; check S = I; adjustment from excess demand.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **AD = 60 + 0.8Y + 40 = 100 + 0.8Y**. Setting AD = Y: Y − 0.8Y = 100, so 0.2Y = 100 and **Y = 500**. Check: **S = −60 + 0.2Y**; at Y = 500, S = −60 + 100 = **40 = I**. Both approaches give ₹500 crore.
(b) At an output of 400, planned spending is **420**, more than output by **20**. Stocks **run down** unexpectedly, so firms **raise output and employment**. Income rises until it reaches **₹500 crore**, where spending and output are equal again.

marking_scheme.step: AD written and set equal to Y
Adjustment: stocks fall, output rises to 500

questions.stem_md: A planning officer in an imagined Odisha district explains the investment multiplier. It is the ratio of

options.text_md: the change in investment to the change in income
total income to total investment
the change in saving to the change in income
the change in income to the change in investment that caused it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the change in income to the change in investment that caused it. k = ΔY ÷ ΔI: how many times income rises for a given rise in investment. ΔS ÷ ΔY is the MPS.

questions.stem_md: Households in an imagined Kerala fishing economy spend nine-tenths of every extra rupee they earn. The value of the investment multiplier is
An economics club in an imagined Indore school debates the possible values of the multiplier. Which statement about its range is correct?

options.text_md: It is 1 when MPC is zero and grows without limit as MPC approaches 1
It lies between 0 and 1
It is always equal to the MPC
It falls as the MPC rises

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is 1 when MPC is zero and grows without limit as MPC approaches 1. k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). With MPC = 0, k = 1 (no extra rounds of spending); as MPC rises towards 1, (1 − MPC) shrinks and k becomes very large.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined hill economy, the multiplier is 4. Its marginal propensity to save must be
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 0.25. k = 1 ÷ MPS, so MPS = 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25 (and MPC = 0.75).

questions.stem_md: A new cement plant raises investment in the imagined economy of Tarangpur (MPC 0.8) by ₹20 crore. By how much will equilibrium income rise?

options.text_md: ₹20 crore
₹16 crore
₹100 crore
₹4 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹100 crore. k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5; ΔY = k × ΔI = 5 × 20 = 100. Income rises from 500 to 600.

questions.stem_md: Private investment in an imagined Tiruchi engineering cluster falls by ₹50 crore, and the regional MPC is 0.6. What happens to the region's income?

options.text_md: It falls by ₹50 crore
It falls by ₹30 crore
It does not change, since the multiplier works only upwards
It falls by ₹125 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It falls by ₹125 crore. The multiplier works in both directions. k = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5; ΔY = 2.5 × (−50) = -125.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The higher the marginal propensity to consume of a community, the larger its investment multiplier.

**Reason (R):** With a higher MPC, a larger share of each round of extra income is spent and becomes someone else's income.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: each round of spending passes a larger fraction on as income, so the sum of all the rounds, k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC), is bigger.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The investment multiplier can be less than one when people save most of their extra income.

**Reason (R):** The multiplier equals the marginal propensity to save.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Even if all extra income is saved (MPS = 1), k = 1 ÷ 1 = 1; it never falls below one. And k is the reciprocal of the MPS, not the MPS itself.

questions.stem_md: True or false? If investment in an imagined Assam tea district falls, the multiplier makes the district's income fall by more than the fall in investment.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The multiplier works backward too: the first fall in income cuts spending, which cuts other incomes in turn, so income falls by k times the fall in investment.

questions.stem_md: The investment multiplier equals 1 divided by the marginal propensity to ___.
questions.solution_md: k = 1 ÷ MPS = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC): one divided by the marginal propensity to save.

questions.stem_md: Explain the meaning of the investment multiplier with an imagined example of a new textile park.
questions.solution_md: Definition with formula and an example.

answer.model_answer_md: The **investment multiplier (k)** is the number of times **income rises** for a given **rise in investment**: **k = ΔY ÷ ΔI**. If a new textile park adds ₹10 crore of investment and income rises by ₹40 crore, **k = 4**.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the multiplier of an imagined thrifty farming community with a high marginal propensity to save is small.
questions.solution_md: Leakage into saving cuts the later rounds.

answer.model_answer_md: k = **1 ÷ MPS**. When the community **saves a large share** of each extra rupee, **less** of it is passed on as spending, so each **round of new income is smaller** and the **total rise in income** is small; a high MPS means a **low k**.

marking_scheme.step: High saving leaks spending, smaller rounds

questions.stem_md: A new metro project adds ₹100 crore of investment in an imagined city economy with MPC 0.8. Show the first three rounds of income generation and find the final rise in income.
questions.solution_md: Rounds of MPC times the previous income; total by the formula.

answer.model_answer_md: **Round 1:** the ₹100 crore becomes income of workers and suppliers. **Round 2:** they spend 0.8 × 100 = **80**, which becomes others' income. **Round 3:** 0.8 × 80 = **64**. The rounds keep shrinking; their sum is **k × ΔI = 5 × 100 = ₹500 crore**.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined Ranchi school claims that the multiplier can take any value from 0 to infinity. Assess her claim, explaining the minimum and maximum values.
questions.solution_md: Range of k from the range of MPC.

answer.model_answer_md: She is **partly wrong**. Since k = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and MPC lies between 0 and 1: when **MPC = 0**, all extra income is saved and **k = 1**, its **minimum**, so it is never below one. As **MPC approaches 1**, the denominator approaches zero and **k becomes very large** (approaching infinity). So k ranges from **1 to infinity**, not from 0.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined state government awards ₹100 crore of road contracts in a region where the MPC is 0.8.

(a) Explain, round by round, how income in the region grows, and find the final rise. [3]
(b) What would the final rise be if the MPC were 0.5? Explain the difference. [2]
questions.solution_md: Rounds with MPC; total by k; compare k at MPC 0.5.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Round 1:** the ₹100 crore is paid as wages and to suppliers; their income rises by 100. **Round 2:** they spend 0.8 of it, **80**, which becomes the income of shopkeepers and farmers. **Round 3:** these spend 0.8 × 80 = **64**, and so on, each round smaller. The total is **k × ΔI = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) × 100 = ₹500 crore**.
(b) With **MPC 0.5**, k = 1 ÷ 0.5 = **2**, so income rises by only **₹200 crore**. More of each rupee is **saved**, so less is passed on in each round and the chain dies out sooner.

questions.stem_md: A labour officer in an imagined Kanpur district says the economy is at full employment. This means that

nobody at all is unemployed, even between jobs
the wage rate is at its highest possible level
everyone able and willing to work at the prevailing wage rate has a job

questions.stem_md: Which of these imagined workers of a Surat diamond town is involuntarily unemployed?

Vikram, who is between two jobs while he shifts to a new workshop

questions.stem_md: According to Keynesian theory, why can the imagined economy of Hiranagar settle at an equilibrium with many people out of work?

options.text_md: Equilibrium always occurs at full employment

questions.stem_md: Define full employment and involuntary unemployment, as they would appear in an imagined Bihar labour report.

questions.stem_md: The imagined economy of Hiranagar is in equilibrium at an income of ₹300 crore, while full employment needs an output of ₹400 crore. Explain why it can stay at ₹300 crore and what this means for workers.

aggregate supply exceeds aggregate demand at full-employment output
prices rise in a year

questions.stem_md: Spending falls short of full-employment output in an imagined Ludhiana manufacturing economy. Which is the most likely result?

questions.stem_md: In the imagined economy of Hiranagar, AD = 120 + 0.6Y and full-employment output is ₹400 crore. What is the gap at full employment?

A deflationary gap of ₹100 crore
No gap, because the economy is in equilibrium

questions.stem_md: An imagined state government wants to reduce excess demand in its economy using fiscal policy. Which step suits this aim?

options.text_md: Raise its own spending on public works

questions.stem_md: Facing deficient demand in an imagined economy, its central bank changes the repo rate. Which direction suits the aim, and why?

A rise, because it raises the money supply

questions.stem_md: To control excess demand, the central bank of an imagined economy raises the cash reserve ratio. How does this help?

options.text_md: Banks can lend more of their deposits

Taxes on consumers are cut

increase total credit in the economy
raise government revenue

options.text_md: True

questions.stem_md: Arrange the chain by which a cut in the repo rate helps an imagined economy facing deficient demand.

questions.stem_md: Suggest two fiscal measures that an imagined state government could take to reduce deficient demand, with a reason for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Raise government spending** on public works such as roads and irrigation: it adds directly to AD and creates incomes.
2. **Cut taxes**: households have more disposable income, so consumption rises.

questions.stem_md: Suggest two quantitative monetary measures the central bank of an imagined economy could use against excess demand, stating the direction of each.
questions.solution_md: Two quantitative tools with the right direction.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Raise the repo rate** (or bank rate): banks pay more for funds, loan rates rise, borrowing and spending fall.
2. **Raise the CRR** (or **sell securities** in open market operations): banks have less money to lend, so credit contracts.

questions.stem_md: Explain three qualitative (selective) credit measures a central bank might use against excess demand for a few scarce goods in an imagined economy.
questions.solution_md: Margin, rationing, moral suasion or direct action.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Margin requirements**: raise the margin on loans against those goods, so borrowers get less credit for hoarding them.
2. **Credit rationing**: limit the total credit banks may give for particular purposes or sectors.
3. **Moral suasion**: persuade banks, through advice and meetings, to go slow on such lending (backed by **direct action** against banks that ignore the advice).

questions.stem_md: The imagined economy of Hiranagar faces a deflationary gap of ₹40 crore with a multiplier of 2.5. A minister proposes extra government spending of ₹100 crore to close the gap. Evaluate the proposal.
questions.solution_md: The gap, not the income shortfall, is the extra spending needed.

answer.model_answer_md: The proposal **overshoots**. With k = 2.5, extra spending of only **₹40 crore** raises income by 2.5 × 40 = **100**, from 300 to full employment at 400. Spending ₹100 crore would raise income by 250 in principle, pushing AD **beyond** full employment and creating **inflationary pressure**. The right amount is the **gap itself**.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined economy at full employment sees prices rising fast after a burst of festival spending financed by easy bank credit.

(a) Identify the problem and explain how it arose. [2]
(b) Suggest three measures, at least one fiscal and one monetary, and explain how each works. [3]
questions.solution_md: Identify excess demand; three correctly directed measures.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) This is **excess demand**: AD is **greater than** full-employment output, an **inflationary gap**. Easy credit let households and traders **spend more** than the economy can produce at full employment, so the extra demand bids up **prices**.
(b) 1. **Fiscal: raise taxes or cut government spending**, which reduces disposable income or public demand and lowers AD.
2. **Monetary: raise the repo rate** or bank rate, so banks charge more for loans and borrowing falls.
3. **Monetary: raise the CRR** or sell government securities, which cuts banks' lending capacity; a selective step such as a **higher margin** on loans against stocks can also curb hoarding.

questions.stem_md:
Factories in an imagined economy are running below capacity and many workers who want jobs cannot find them.

(a) Identify the problem and describe it on a diagram. [2]
(b) Recommend three measures to correct it and justify each, commenting on which is likely to act fastest. [3]
questions.solution_md: Deficient demand; diagram; three measures with a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) This is **deficient demand**: AD **falls short** of full-employment output, a **deflationary gap**. On the income–expenditure diagram, AD cuts the forty-five degree line **to the left** of full-employment output; at full employment, the vertical gap between the forty-five degree line and AD is the deflationary gap.
(b) 1. **More government spending** on public works: it adds to AD at once and, through the multiplier, raises income by more than the spending.
2. **Tax cuts**: households keep more income and spend more.
3. **Cheaper credit**: cut the repo rate and CRR, or buy securities, so banks lend more. Direct public spending usually works **fastest**, because firms may not borrow even when credit is cheap if they expect weak sales.

questions.solution_md: Name and effect; one measure of each kind.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It is **excess demand**, also called an **inflationary gap**. The economy is already at full employment, so there are no idle workers or machines and **real output cannot rise**; the extra spending only bids up the **general price level**, and money incomes lose purchasing power.
(ii) **Fiscal**: the government can **raise taxes** or **cut its own spending**, which leaves less money to spend and lowers AD. **Monetary**: the central bank can **raise the repo rate** or the **CRR**, so loans become dearer and scarcer, borrowing falls and spending is curbed.

questions.stem_md:

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Full employment** is the situation in which **everyone able and willing to work at the prevailing wage** has a job. It does **not** mean zero unemployment: people **changing jobs** (frictional) or **choosing not to work** may still be idle.
(ii) A worker who **accepts the going wage** but **finds no job** is **involuntarily unemployed**. Keynes argued that output is set by **aggregate demand**; if planned spending is low, the economy settles at an **equilibrium below full employment**, so such unemployment can **persist**.

Below the axis, the saving line (from −60) meets the horizontal investment line at the **same income**.
(ii) k = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = **5**; ΔY = 5 × 20 = **100**; new income **₹600 crore**. The extra ₹20 crore is paid out as **income** to workers and suppliers; they spend **0.8** of it, which becomes others' income, who again spend 0.8 of that. These **shrinking rounds** add up to 5 times the first injection, because **0.2** of each round leaks into saving.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) In the imagined economy of Hiranagar, AD = 120 + 0.6Y and full-employment output is ₹400 crore. Find the gap, explain its effects and show how much extra spending would close it.

questions.solution_md: Gap, effects, needed spending; comparison and recommended mix.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **AD at 400** = 120 + 240 = **360**: a **deflationary gap of ₹40 crore**. Income settles at **₹300 crore**, so output and employment are below full employment and willing workers stay jobless.
